claims.text: High-entropy nanoalloys maintain structural and chemical stability at high temperatures because of dynamic vacancy-mediated interdiffusion.
Vacancy-mediated interdiffusion sustains atomic-scale chemical homogeneity.
Dynamic atomic mixing counteracts the thermodynamic drive for phase segregation.
The initial nanoalloys have a homogeneous, random distribution of multiple principal elements.
Elevated-temperature vacuum annealing generates and mobilizes vacancies in the nanoalloys.
Temperature-induced vacancies activate both surface and bulk diffusion pathways.
Vacancy-activated diffusion enables continuous atomic mixing.
Continuous atomic mixing self-heals local compositional fluctuations.
Annealing increases vacancy formation at both the surface and in the bulk.
Increased surface and bulk vacancy formation promotes rapid atomic interdiffusion.
Vacancy-driven dynamic mixing preserves crystal-lattice integrity.
Under in situ vacuum annealing, high-entropy nanoalloys will exhibit minimal compositional segregation.
Under in situ vacuum annealing, high-entropy nanoalloys will maintain a uniform lattice structure over time.
Conventional binary or multiphase alloys will exhibit more noticeable phase separation than high-entropy nanoalloys under the same annealing conditions.
Conventional binary or multiphase alloys will exhibit greater structural degradation than high-entropy nanoalloys under the same annealing conditions.
The stabilizing effect applies only in a moderate high-temperature window in which vacancy generation enhances interdiffusion without causing rapid morphological deterioration.
Above the proposed optimal temperature window, excessive vacancy generation may cause coarsening or other degradation.
